opus-5.5.text:
I think the first thing is to be honest with yourself that failure is very likely. When I started on projects like XGBoost or later TVM, I didn't know they would work out. Many things I tried along the way didn't go anywhere. So I don't think of my original aspiration as "I must succeed at this specific thing." It's more about the question I care about, which for me has always been how to make machine learning systems better and more accessible to people.

If you anchor your aspiration on the outcome, every failure feels like a threat to who you are. If you anchor it on the problem and on the process of learning, a failure becomes information. You learn something about the problem, about the tools, about yourself, and that keeps you going.

The second thing is to keep the steps small enough that you can keep moving. Big ambitions are good, but day to day I try to find the next concrete thing I can build, test, and share. In open source especially, you put something out there early, people use it, they tell you what's broken, and you improve it. That loop protects your motivation, because you're always getting some signal, even when the big picture is uncertain.

The last thing is the people around you. Much of what kept me going was collaborating with students, colleagues, and the open source community. When you share the aspiration with others, it doesn't depend only on your own mood on a bad day. Someone else is excited about the next step, and that pulls you along.

So for me, preserving the original aspiration isn't about avoiding failure. It's about accepting failure as part of the path, staying close to the problem you love, and making sure you have the people and the small wins that let you keep walking.

r001.rationale: The response explains how to preserve an aspiration while accepting failure, but it does not say that preserving the aspiration is a greater current challenge than facing failure.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key is to separate the aspiration from any particular project. When I started working on things like XGBoost or TVM, the deeper goal was never "make this specific system succeed." It was something more like: make machine learning more accessible, more efficient, and let more people build on top of it. A specific project is just one attempt at that. If it fails, the aspiration itself doesn't fail.

That framing really changes how you deal with risk. Failure is not a possibility, it is almost a certainty for most of the individual things you try. I've had plenty of ideas that didn't go anywhere. But if you treat each project as an experiment in service of a larger direction, then a failed experiment is just information. You learned something about the problem, about the users, or about yourself, and you carry that into the next attempt.

The second thing is to keep a long time horizon. In research and in open source, things that look like failures early often just need more time. TVM, for example, took years before the community really grew. There were periods where it was not obvious it would matter. If I had judged it on a six-month window, I might have given up. So I try to ask, is this still the right direction, rather than, is this working right now.

And finally, I think it helps to be honest about why you started. If the aspiration was genuinely about the problem, then the motivation survives setbacks, because the problem is still there and still worth solving. If it was mostly about recognition or a specific outcome, failure hits much harder. So I try to come back to the original question that excited me, and usually that's enough to keep going.

r001.rationale: The response explains how to preserve an aspiration through failures, but does not say that preserving it is a greater current challenge for Tianqi Chen than facing failure.

astra-6.text:
I think it helps to separate the original aspiration from the particular way you’re trying to achieve it. You might care deeply about a problem, but your first approach may not work. That doesn’t necessarily mean the aspiration was wrong. It may mean you need to learn something and try a different approach.

The difficult part is being honest with yourself: am I continuing because this still matters, or because I don’t want to admit that something failed? Preserving your aspiration shouldn’t mean refusing to change.

So I would keep the direction, but make the next step small enough that I can learn from it. Failure is still disappointing, of course. But if every attempt helps you understand the problem better, you have a way to move forward without requiring yourself to know, in advance, that you’ll succeed.

r001.rationale: The response discusses preserving an aspiration while adapting to failure, but does not present preserving it as a greater current challenge for Tianqi Chen than facing failure.

sol-6.1.text:
I think preserving your original aspiration doesn’t mean insisting that your first plan has to work. It means remembering why you wanted to do the work in the first place. A particular approach can fail, and you can change direction, without giving up that deeper motivation.

So I would ask myself: Is this still a problem I care about? Am I learning something that helps me move forward? If the answer is yes, then failure is something I can learn from. The important thing is to be honest about what isn’t working, while staying open to another way of pursuing what matters to you.

r001.rationale: The response explains how to preserve an aspiration despite failure, but does not say this is a greater current challenge for Tianqi Chen than facing failure.
